title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 1: Chemical Reactions and Equations
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: A complete chemical equation represents the reactants, products and their physical states symbolically. A chemical equation is balanced so that the numbers of atoms of each type involved in a chemical reaction are the same on the reactant and product sides of the equation. Equations must always be balanced to satisfy the Law of Conservation of Mass: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Example: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g).

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 1: Chemical Reactions and Equations
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: In a combination reaction two or more substances combine to form a new single substance. Decomposition reactions are opposite to combination reactions: a single substance decomposes to give two or more substances. Reactions in which heat is given out along with the products are called exothermic reactions. Reactions in which energy is absorbed are known as endothermic reactions. When an element displaces another element from its compound, a displacement reaction occurs: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds in a double displacement reaction: Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq).

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 2: Acids, Bases and Salts
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
section: 2.1 Understanding the Chemical Properties of Acids and Bases
excerpt: Acids are sour in taste and change the colour of blue litmus to red. Bases are bitter and change the colour of red litmus to blue. Litmus solution is a purple dye extracted from lichen. When an acid reacts with a metal, hydrogen gas is evolved and a corresponding salt is formed: Acid + Metal -> Salt + Hydrogen gas. For example, 2HCl + Zn -> ZnCl2 + H2. When acids react with metal carbonates or hydrogen carbonates, carbon dioxide gas is produced: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 2: Acids, Bases and Salts
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
section: 2.2 What do all acids and all bases have in common?
excerpt: All acids generate hydrogen ions H+(aq) in solution, which are responsible for their acidic properties. In dry conditions, dry HCl gas does not dissociate and cannot change dry blue litmus paper. Hydrogen ions cannot exist alone, but they exist after combining with water molecules: H+ + H2O -> H3O+ (hydronium ion). When a base is dissolved in water, it produces hydroxide ions OH-(aq). Bases which are soluble in water are called alkalis (e.g., NaOH, KOH).

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 2: Acids, Bases and Salts
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
section: 2.3 How Strong are Acid or Base Solutions? (The pH Scale)
excerpt: A scale for measuring hydrogen ion concentration in a solution is called the pH scale. The p in pH stands for 'potenz' in German, meaning power. On the pH scale we can measure pH from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very alkaline). Neutral solution has a pH of 7. Values less than 7 represent an acidic solution. As the pH value increases from 7 to 14, it represents an increase in OH- ion concentration in the solution. Diluting an acid or a base means mixing it with water; this results in a decrease in the concentration of ions (H3O+/OH-) per unit volume. For an acid, diluting with water decreases [H3O+] per unit volume, which increases the pH towards 7.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 11: Electricity
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: Electric current is expressed by the amount of charge flowing through a particular area in unit time. In other words, it is the rate of flow of electric charges. In circuits using metallic wires, electrons constitute the flow of charges. If a net charge Q, flows across any cross-section of a conductor in time t, then the current I, through the cross-section is I = Q/t. The SI unit of electric charge is coulomb (C). The electric current is expressed by a unit called ampere (A), named after French scientist Andre-Marie Ampere. One ampere is constituted by the flow of one coulomb of charge per second, that is, 1 A = 1 C / 1 s.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 11: Electricity
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: In 1827, German physicist Georg Simon Ohm found out the relationship between the current I flowing in a metallic wire and the potential difference across its terminals. Ohm's Law: The potential difference, V, across the ends of a given metallic wire in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided its temperature remains the same. Mathematically, V ∝ I or V/I = constant = R, or V = IR. R is a constant for the given metallic wire at a given temperature and is called its resistance. It is the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges through it. Its SI unit is ohm, represented by the Greek letter Ω. According to Ohm's law, R = V/I. If the potential difference across the two ends of a conductor is 1 V and the current through it is 1 A, then the resistance R, of the conductor is 1 Ω. That is, 1 ohm = 1 volt / 1 ampere.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 11: Electricity
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: If the electric circuit is purely resistive, that is, a configuration of resistors only connected to a battery; the source energy continually gets dissipated entirely in the form of heat. This is known as the heating effect of electric current. Consider a current I flowing through a resistor of resistance R. Let the potential difference across it be V. The work done in moving the charge Q through potential difference V in time t is W = V x Q = V x I x t. Therefore, the heat energy produced is H = V x I x t = I^2 x R x t. This is known as Joule's law of heating. The law implies that heat produced in a resistor is: (i) directly proportional to the square of current for a given resistance, (ii) directly proportional to resistance for a given current, and (iii) directly proportional to the time for which the current flows through the resistor.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 5: Life Processes
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: Life processes are the basic vital processes essential for maintaining an organism's life: nutrition, respiration, transportation, and excretion. In autotrophic nutrition, green plants take in CO2 and H2O and convert them into carbohydrates in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight: 6CO2 + 12H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. Photosynthesis involves three main events: (i) absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, (ii) conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, (iii) reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates. Stomata are tiny pores present on the surface of leaves through which massive amounts of gaseous exchange take place; their opening and closing is regulated by guard cells which swell when water flows into them. In heterotrophic nutrition, humans ingest food through the alimentary canal: saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase which breaks down starch into simple sugar maltose; the stomach secretes gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, protein-digesting enzyme pepsin, and mucus; the small intestine is the site of complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, aided by bile juice from the liver and pancreatic juice containing trypsin and lipase; the inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called villi that increase the surface area for absorption.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 5: Life Processes
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: Respiration involves the breakdown of glucose to release energy for cellular activities. In the first step, a 6-carbon molecule glucose is broken down in the cytoplasm into a 3-carbon molecule called pyruvate (glycolysis). This pyruvate may follow three distinct pathways: (1) In absence of oxygen (anaerobic respiration in yeast during fermentation), pyruvate is converted into ethanol, carbon dioxide, and energy; (2) In lack of oxygen in human muscle cells during strenuous exercise, pyruvate is converted into 3-carbon lactic acid, causing cramps; (3) In presence of oxygen (aerobic respiration in mitochondria), pyruvate breaks down to yield carbon dioxide, water, and a large amount of energy in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate). In human respiratory systems, air enters through nostrils, passes through the trachea supported by rings of cartilage, and reaches the lungs where passage divides into smaller tubes ending in balloon-like structures called alveoli. Alveoli provide an extensive surface for gaseous exchange; respiratory pigment hemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen in the lungs and delivers it to oxygen-deficient tissues.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 5: Life Processes
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: The human heart is a muscular organ with four chambers: two atria and two ventricles, preventing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Blood flows through the heart twice during each cycle (double circulation: pulmonary and systemic). Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and have thick elastic walls; veins bring blood back to the heart at lower pressure and have valves to ensure unidirectional flow. In plants, xylem tissues (vessels and tracheids) transport water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves driven by root pressure and transpiration pull; phloem transports soluble products of photosynthesis (translocation, mainly sucrose) to storage organs and growing regions using metabolic energy from ATP. The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder, and a urethra. The structural and functional filtration unit of the kidney is the nephron, each consisting of a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule enclosing a tuft of capillaries called the glomerulus. As the initial filtrate passes through the tubular part of the nephron, substances like glucose, amino acids, mineral salts, and a major amount of water are selectively reabsorbed into surrounding capillaries, leaving urine which is stored in the urinary bladder.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 9: Light - Reflection and Refraction
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: Light travels in straight lines in a homogeneous medium. The laws of reflection: (1) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r); (2) The incident ray, the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray, all lie in the same plane. In spherical mirrors, the reflecting surface can be curved inward (concave mirror, converging) or curved outward (convex mirror, diverging). The distance between the pole and principal focus is the focal length f; for spherical mirrors of small aperture, the radius of curvature R is twice the focal length (R = 2f). The mirror formula expresses the relationship between object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f): 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m produced by a spherical mirror is given by m = height of image (h') / height of object (h) = -v/u. A concave mirror produces real and inverted images for object positions beyond the focus, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when placed between focus and pole.

title: NCERT Class 10 Science - Chapter 9: Light - Reflection and Refraction
publisher: National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT)
subject: Science
excerpt: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent optical medium to another due to change in speed. Laws of refraction: (1) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane; (2) Snell's law: The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to sine of angle of refraction is a constant for light of a given colour and given pair of media: sin(i)/sin(r) = constant = n21 (refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1). Absolute refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum (c) / speed of light in medium (v). The lens formula relating object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) for spherical lenses is: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification produced by a lens is m = h'/h = v/u. The power of a lens (P) is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres: P = 1/f(m). The SI unit of power of a lens is dioptre (D); 1 dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre (1 D = 1 m^-1). Power of a converging convex lens is positive, while that of a diverging concave lens is negative.
